record.narrative: Wave 1 registers a broad set of falsifiable associations between measured genomic/biomarker predictors and CRISPR dependency scores, prioritizing biologically plausible biomarker-outcome pairings across all requested dependency outcomes. Direction convention is that more negative dependency means stronger dependency. Driver-alteration hypotheses expect enhanced dependency on the corresponding driver or downstream effector: KRAS mutation and stronger KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E and stronger BRAF dependency; EGFR amplification and stronger EGFR dependency; ERBB2 amplification and stronger ERBB2 dependency. Tumor suppressor/pathway hypotheses expect pathway-specific dependencies: KEAP1 loss and stronger NFE2L2 dependency; TP53 loss and weaker MDM2 dependency because MDM2 is most important when p53 is intact; SMARCA4/ARID1A loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency as synthetic-lethal remodeling dependencies; MSI-high or BRCA2 loss and stronger WRN dependency under DNA-repair stress hypotheses. MYC amplification is tested against core transcription/translation/stress-response dependencies (POLR2A, RPL11, DHX9, USP7) to capture broad oncogenic transcriptional addiction and alternative MYC-stabilization pathways. KRAS mutation is tested against RIT1 with a weaker-dependency hypothesis because mutant KRAS may reduce reliance on upstream RIT1 signaling, while alternative models are possible. RB1 loss is tested against KIF18A because E2F-driven cell-cycle entry could increase dependence on mitotic kinesin function. PIK3CA mutation is tested against STAT3 because PI3K/AKT signaling can cooperate with STAT3. ERBB2 amplification is tested against TMED10 as a weaker secretory-trafficking dependence hypothesis. These are discovery associations only; none imply causality or generalizability until evidence and validation are assessed.

Selected 12 discovery comparisons that cover many requested outcomes while prioritizing high-prior biological associations. Driver-specific claims H1-H4 test whether pathway-associated genomic alterations correspond to dependency on the same driver or effector. H5 and H6 test canonical pathway logic for KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2 and TP53 loss/MDM2. H7 tests synthetic-lethal chromatin-remodeling dependence, and H9 tests MSI-high/WRN. MYC amplification is probed through transcription and translation dependencies H11 and H12. H15 and H17 extend to pathway-level dependencies for KRAS/RIT1 and PIK3CA/STAT3. Deferred duplicate SMARCA2 and WRN claims (H8, H10), additional MYC outcomes (H13, H14), and lower-prior KIF18A/TMED10 claims (H16, H18) so that later waves can be allocated based on observed effect sizes and uncertainty.

Wave-1 discovery supports three very large, precise associations, but only two are in the registered hypothesized direction. H7 is accepted: SMARCA4 loss is associated with substantially stronger SMARCA2 dependency, signed estimate +0.784 with 95% interval entirely positive under direction -1. H9 is accepted: MSI-high is associated with substantially stronger WRN dependency, signed estimate +0.790 with interval entirely positive under direction -1. Because these are CRISPR dependency scores, more negative raw scores mean stronger dependency; these signed positive values under direction -1 correspond to raw negative differences, i.e., stronger dependency in the exposed groups. The magnitudes are far above the 10% clinical-significance scale relative to outcome means. H5 is rejected as originally registered. Its signed estimate is -0.796 with a 95% interval entirely negative under direction -1, so the data strongly favor the opposite raw contrast: KEAP1-loss cells have dependency_NFE2L2 that is about 0.796 units higher/less negative than KEAP1-wild-type cells. This is a very large association, but its sign contradicts the registered hypothesis that KEAP1 loss would produce stronger NFE2L2 dependency. The correct response is to register a reversed association proposal and independently validate the original comparison to check whether this anomalous direction is reproducible or reflects scale/coding/constructed-data behavior. H3 is borderline and remains unresolved: EGFR amplification has a point estimate of about 0.025 units of stronger EGFR dependency, roughly 10% of the outcome mean, but the signed interval includes zero, so multiplicity-adjusted or independent confirmation is needed before acceptance. The remaining driver and pathway hypotheses (H1, H2, H4, H6, H11, H12, H15, H17) show small signed effects with intervals crossing zero and generally near-null magnitudes; they are not accepted. Some remain active because driver hypotheses deserve focused follow-up, while lower-prior or untested claims are deferred. The follow-up proposals test whether the accepted effects are subtype-specific or confounded by correlated genomic markers (ARID1A loss for SMARCA4, KRAS mutation for EGFR) and whether the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association remains after removing TP53-loss cells.

The independent validation result R13 resolves the KEAP1/NFE2L2 sign anomaly. For the originally registered claim H5, with direction -1 (expected stronger NFE2L2 dependency under KEAP1 loss), validation gives signed estimate -0.7914, interval [-0.8213, -0.7615], entirely negative under the original direction. This confirms that the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive: KEAP1-loss cells have higher, less negative dependency_NFE2L2 than KEAP1-intact cells. Therefore the original hypothesis is rejected in this dataset, not merely unresolved. Because validation also supports the reversed association H19, with signed estimate +0.7914 and strict independent interval entirely positive under direction +1, I accept H19 as a dataset-level association: KEAP1 loss is associated with substantially weaker NFE2L2 dependency by about 0.79 dependency units, with discovery and validation estimates +0.796 and +0.791 respectively and intervals excluding zero. The magnitude is more than two outcome SDs and far above the 10% meaningful-scale threshold, although relative-difference interpretation is awkward because the overall outcome mean is close to zero. This remains an association, not evidence of causality or general biological behavior. I close H5 and the primary reversed claim H19 because the comparison is now well characterized in this dataset, while new proposals test context specificity and possible confounding.

The accepted wave-1 discoveries H7 and H9 remain important. SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency. However, neither has independent validation yet, and it is unclear whether these effects are stable across lineage subtype, culture type, correlated chromatin-remodeling losses, or other dataset structure. I therefore propose focused interaction and conditional analyses: lineage/culture heterogeneity for H7 and H9; ARID1A-loss heterogeneity for the SMARCA2 claim; and TP53-loss/lineage heterogeneity for the reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association. I also propose research_marker_e_positive controls for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2. Because research_marker_e is a constructed binary assay with no assigned biological role, null associations for this marker would support specificity of the accepted effects; strong associations would indicate that the dataset may encode broader structure or technical confounding.

The remaining driver claims are still not accepted. H1 KRAS mutation remains near but not statistically convincing for stronger KRAS dependency; H3 EGFR amplification is borderline with signed estimate about +0.025 under direction -1 and interval crossing zero. I propose subtype follow-ups for KRAS and EGFR, while EGFR-specific KRAS-wild-type and adenocarcinoma subgroup claims already registered can be analyzed next. The next analysis should prioritize the registered H19 refinements, accepted-effect interaction tests, specificity controls, and EGFR/KRAS follow-ups. In the next appraise, if discovery evidence remains favorable, I plan to request independent validation for H7 or H9, starting with SMARCA4 loss as the most direct synthetic-lethality-like dataset association, then WRN/MSI-high in a later validation cycle.

The next exploration wave focuses on three goals: (1) stress-test the accepted dataset associations, (2) probe whether near-null driver hypotheses are masked by lineage or constructed-marker structure, and (3) broaden coverage of outcomes that have not yet been analyzed. For the accepted effects, I register research_marker_d_positive as a constructed binary negative control. If marker D shows a large association with SMARCA2 or WRN, or an accepted effect changes materially across marker D-positive and marker D-negative cells, this would suggest that the large effects may partly reflect dataset encoding, confounding, or marker-correlated population structure rather than isolated genomic-loss associations. If marker D is near null and the accepted interaction differences are small, that increases confidence that the associations are specific to the genomic markers of interest. I likewise register media_serum_pct interactions to test whether serum condition modifies the SMARCA4/SMARCA2, MSI-high/WRN, and KEAP1/NFE2L2 associations; this addresses whether these associations are robust across culture conditions. For near-null driver hypotheses, I add subtype-specific comparisons for BRAF V600E and ERBB2 amplification in adenocarcinoma, and marker-interaction tests for EGFR amplification and KRAS mutation. These are not claims of causality; they are diagnostics for heterogeneity and possible dataset confounding. I also reactivate deferred but biologically motivated comparisons, including ARID1A loss versus SMARCA2, BRCA2 loss versus WRN, MYC amplification versus DHX9/USP7, RB1 loss versus KIF18A, and ERBB2 amplification versus TMED10, so that the next analysis wave can still cover less-tested outcome-predictor pairs if the controller selects them.

I am allocating the next 12 discovery analyses to stress-test the three currently accepted dataset associations rather than immediately expanding to lower-priority driver hypotheses. The accepted associations are very large in this dataset, but I want to determine whether they are marker-specific, robust across major context variables, and not primarily driven by constructed assay structure or correlated genomic losses. For each accepted association, I run a constructed binary negative control and its interaction: research_marker_d_positive versus the outcome, and accepted_exposure effect marker_d_positive versus marker_d_negative. If marker D shows a large independent association with SMARCA2, WRN, or NFE2L2 dependency, or if the accepted effect differs materially across marker D-positive and marker D-negative cells, this would temper confidence that the accepted association is specific to the genomic marker and raise concern about dataset encoding or confounding. If marker D is near null and the accepted interactions are small, that supports specificity and homogeneity. I also test context specificity: SMARCA2 loss effects in the adenocarcinoma subtype and after restricting to ARID1A-intact cells, WRN/MSI-high effects in adenocarcinoma and across adenocarcinoma versus non-adenocarcinoma, and KEAP1/NFE2L2 effects separately in TP53-intact and TP53-loss cells. The ARID1A-intact restriction is particularly important for SMARCA2 because ARID1A loss is biologically correlated with SWI/SNF remodeling loss and could contribute to the SMARCA4 association. The TP53 splits are important because KEAP1 and TP53 alterations may co-occur and the reversed NFE2L2 association could be concentrated in one genomic context. If these analyses remain consistently large and homogeneous, the next appraise is a good place to request independent validation for SMARCA4 loss versus SMARCA2 dependency, followed by MSI-high versus WRN if resources allow.

This wave materially strengthens the specificity and robustness of the three currently accepted dataset associations. The constructed negative control research_marker_d_positive is near null for all three outcomes: SMARCA2 (R14), WRN (R15), and NFE2L2 (R16). Although these are not equivalence proofs, the point estimates are small relative to the main effects and the 95% intervals cross zero, so there is no evidence for a marker-D-specific association. Likewise, the marker-D interaction tests on the accepted effects are near null: SMARCA4/SMARCA2 (R17), MSI-high/WRN (R18), and KEAP1/NFE2L2 (R19). The adenocarcinoma interaction for MSI-high/WRN is also small and imprecise around zero (R23), consistent with a broadly shared effect rather than a subtype-restricted one. These results reduce concern that the large associations are driven by random dataset structure correlated with marker D. Conditional analyses also remain very large: SMARCA4-loss cells in adenocarcinoma (R20) and SMARCA4-loss cells restricted to ARID1A-intact cells (R21) both show signed effects about 0.78 under direction -1, meaning raw SMARCA2 dependency is roughly 0.78 units more negative than in the comparator group. MSI-high cells in adenocarcinoma similarly show about 0.78 signed effect under direction -1 (R22). The reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is present and large in both TP53-intact (R24) and TP53-loss (R25) cells, with signed estimates about 0.79 and 0.81 under direction +1, meaning raw NFE2L2 dependency is higher/less negative in KEAP1-loss cells by about the same magnitude in both genomic contexts. I therefore accept these conditional/subgroup associations as dataset-specific evidence: SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency in the adenocarcinoma subtype and independently of ARID1A loss; MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency in the adenocarcinoma subtype; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency in both TP53-intact and TP53-loss cells. I reject the marker-D and heterogeneity interaction claims because their estimates are negligible and intervals include zero. Given that the SMARCA4/SMARCA2 claim has the largest cell counts among accepted primary associations and has survived the main confounding checks, I request independent validation for H7 before validating WRN/MSI-high. These conclusions remain dataset associations, not causal or generalizable findings.

The independent validation result for H7 is strongly supportive. Under the registered direction -1, validation R26 gives a signed estimate of +0.8006 with an independent interval entirely positive, [0.7713, 0.8300], at alpha=0.003846. Because the estimate is already signed to the hypothesis direction, the raw SMARCA4-loss minus SMARCA4-intact difference in dependency_SMARCA2 is approximately -0.80, meaning SMARCA4-loss cells have substantially more negative dependency_SMARCA2 scores, i.e., stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Discovery R7 was consistent: signed estimate +0.7840, interval [0.7646, 0.8034]. The validation estimate is nearly identical to discovery and the independent interval excludes zero even under a stringent multiplicity-adjusted threshold. The magnitude is very large: it is more than two outcome SDs and far exceeds the 10% meaningful-difference threshold, although relative-difference framing is awkward because dependency scores are centered near zero. I therefore accept H7 as a robust, independently validated dataset-level association: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. I close H7 as the primary claim because the direction and magnitude are now well characterized in this dataset. This association is biologically plausible as a synthetic-lethality-like relationship, but the data remain associational; they do not establish causality or generalizability beyond this dataset. The most informative next analysis is independent validation of H9, MSI-high versus WRN dependency, which is the next accepted but not yet independently validated large effect. Negative findings from prior robustness tests remain meaningful: the original H5 KEAP1/NFE2L2 hypothesis is rejected and reversed H19 is validated; marker-D negative controls and marker-D interactions for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2 are null/close-to-null; and the WRN subtype interaction is null. Conditional accepted subgroup effects for SMARCA2 and WRN remain consistent but are not independently validated and should be interpreted only as dataset-specific subgroup associations. Many driver-gene hypotheses remain unresolved or unresolved near-null and should not be presented as supported.

This wave focuses on three goals: stress-test the newly validated SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 dependency association, prepare the MSI-high/WRN association for validation, and test whether near-null MAPK driver associations are masked by mutual-exclusivity structure. First, I add research_marker_f_positive as a second constructed binary negative control for WRN, SMARCA2, and NFE2L2. Marker D was near null and did not materially modify the main effects; analogous marker-F nulls would reduce concern that the large effects are artifacts of arbitrary constructed marker encoding or marker-correlated population structure. Second, I add screen_batch interactions for the major accepted associations. A near-null batch interaction would support stability across screen-batch structure, whereas a large interaction would indicate that the apparent effect is partly confounded by technical or dataset batch structure. Third, I add context-specific checks: ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells to test whether the SMARCA2 dependency signal is specific to SMARCA4 loss rather than generalized SWI/SNF loss; BRCA2 loss among MSI-negative cells to test whether WRN dependency reflects DNA-repair biology beyond MSI-high status; adherent-culture MSI-high/WRN effect as a direct robustness check for the pending H9 validation; and KRAS or BRAF driver effects restricted to the other mutually exclusive wild-type context to ask whether the near-null MAPK associations are diluted by co-occurrence structure. All hypotheses remain dataset associations rather than causal claims.

I select twelve discovery analyses that most directly stress-test the currently accepted dataset associations before requesting independent validation for MSI-high/WRN. For each major association (SMARCA4 loss/SMARCA2, MSI-high/WRN, KEAP1 loss/NFE2L2), I run marker F negative-control main effects and marker F interactions. Marker D controls and marker D interactions were near null; a consistent marker F null pattern would reduce concern that the large effects are artifacts of arbitrary constructed-marker encoding or marker-correlated structure. I also run screen_batch_a interactions for all three accepted exposures to assess whether the effects are stable across screen batch rather than driven by batch-correlated structure. I include the adherent-culture MSI-high/WRN main effect as a direct context-specific robustness check before validation. Finally, I include two specificity checks: ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells to test whether SMARCA2 dependency is specific to SMARCA4 loss rather than generalized SWI/SNF-loss biology, and BRCA2 loss among MSI-negative cells to test whether WRN dependency has DNA-repair associations beyond MSI-high status. I defer the lower-priority mutual-exclusivity-restricted KRAS/BRAF driver tests because they concern currently near-null driver claims and are less important than validating the robustness of the three large accepted associations.

This wave adds marker-F negative controls, batch interaction tests, an adherent-culture MSI-high/WRN analysis, and two specificity analyses. The marker-F controls are close to null for all three major outcomes: WRN (R27), SMARCA2 (R31), and NFE2L2 (R35). The marker-F interactions with the accepted associations are also near null for SMARCA2 (R32), WRN (R28), and NFE2L2 (R36). Together with the earlier marker-D null controls and null interactions, these results reduce concern that the very large SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, MSI-high/WRN, and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 associations are artifacts of arbitrary constructed-marker structure or marker-correlated population structure. Batch tests for MSI-high/WRN and KEAP1/NFE2L2 are near null (R29, R37), although the WRN batch interaction is imprecise because the exposed cells in batch_a are small. The SMARCA2 batch_a interaction is statistically nonzero but small in magnitude and opposite to the registered negative-direction claim; it does not support the claim as registered and is far smaller than the main SMARCA4 effect, so I reject it for that claim rather than treating it as a meaningful confounder. The adherent-culture MSI-high/WRN effect is very large and precise (R30: signed estimate +0.813, 95% CI [0.780,0.846] under direction -1), consistent with the overall MSI-high/WRN effect (R8) and the adenocarcinoma-restricted effect (R22). The ARID1A-loss effect among SMARCA4-intact cells is null (R34), supporting specificity of the SMARCA2 signal to SMARCA4 loss rather than generalized SWI/SNF loss. The BRCA2-loss effect among MSI-negative cells is null (R38), suggesting the WRN association is not a broad DNA-repair-loss marker but is more specific to MSI-high status in this dataset. Given this robustness pattern, I request independent validation for H9, MSI-high versus WRN dependency, because it is the next accepted large association and has now survived marker controls, subtype, culture, and specificity checks.

The newly delivered validation strengthens the main set of supported dataset-specific associations. For H5, the original hypothesis that KEAP1 loss is associated with stronger NFE2L2 dependency remains rejected. The independent validation R13, registered under direction -1, is signed negative, estimate -0.791 with an independent interval entirely negative, [-0.821, -0.761]. Because estimates are already signed to the registered direction, this negative result indicates that the raw KEAP1-loss minus KEAP1-intact difference in dependency_NFE2L2 is positive: KEAP1-loss cells have higher, less negative dependency_NFE2L2 scores. Thus validation confirms the direction reversal captured by H19 rather than the original H5 direction. For H9, independent validation R39 strongly supports the MSI-high association: signed estimate +0.8215 with an independent interval entirely positive, [0.766, 0.877], at the validation alpha threshold. This is consistent with discovery R8, signed estimate +0.7899. The raw interpretation is that MSI-high cells have dependency_WRN scores about 0.82 units lower, i.e. much stronger WRN dependency. The magnitude is more than three WRN outcome SDs and far exceeds a 10% relative-difference threshold when interpreted cautiously, although relative ratios are awkward because dependency scores are centered near zero. H9 is therefore accepted as an independently validated dataset-level association and closed as a primary claim. For H20, independent validation R40 supports the TP53-intact KEAP1 context: signed estimate +0.7948 with independent interval [0.764, 0.826], consistent with discovery R24. This confirms that the KEAP1-loss association with weaker NFE2L2 dependency is large in TP53-intact cells, while prior discovery H26 indicates a similar large effect in TP53-loss cells, though H26 itself has not been independently validated. Overall supported associations now include: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, validated by R7/R26; MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, validated by R8/R39; and KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, validated in the reversed H19 and in the TP53-intact conditional H20. The accepted set also includes large conditional/context claims: SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency in adenocarcinoma and ARID1A-intact cells; MSI-high WRN dependency in adenocarcinoma and adherent culture; and KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 dependency in TP53-loss cells. Negative and robustness findings remain meaningful: original H5 is rejected; marker D and marker F constructed controls are near null for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2; marker D/F interactions are near null; the WRN subtype interaction is null; ARID1A loss in SMARCA4-intact cells is null for SMARCA2; and BRCA2 loss in MSI-negative cells is null for WRN. The most informative next work is to complete the marker-E control suite, test media-serum and other culture/technical contexts, and continue to probe remaining driver and MYC-associated hypotheses without claiming causality or generalizability. All conclusions remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or external-validity claims.

This wave adds focused robustness and context checks for the three large accepted associations: SMARCA4 loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency. First, I register main effects within the dominant Avana library and, where cell numbers are expected to be adequate, within the KY library. These library-specific effects test whether the associations are library-dependent or persist across CRISPR screen platforms. For SMARCA2 and NFE2L2, I also register Avana-versus-non-Avana interactions to test technical stability. For WRN, I avoid a library interaction because MSI-high is a relatively small exposed group and the non-Avana exposed cell could fall below the required cell count. Second, I register interactions with proliferation rate, mutation burden, ploidy, and 10% serum media context to test whether the accepted effects are stable after stratification on cell-state and genomic-instability proxies. A near-null interaction would support robustness; a large interaction would indicate that the effect is concentrated in particular proliferative, mutational, ploidy, or serum contexts. Third, I add a STK11 co-loss interaction for the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association because KEAP1 and STK11 co-loss biology is common in lung adenocarcinoma-like lines; a null interaction would make the KEAP1 association less likely to be a co-loss artifact. These proposals complement already registered marker-E controls, marker-E interactions, culture-type adherence checks, media 5% main effects, and media 10% interactions. All remain dataset-specific associations and are not causal or generalizability claims.

No assessments are due, so I use the analysis slot to stress-test the currently accepted large dataset associations and complete the constructed-marker control suite. First, I request marker-E main effects for the three major outcomes: SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-loss cells (H34), WRN dependency among MSI-high cells (H35), and NFE2L2 dependency among KEAP1-loss cells (H36). Marker D and marker F main effects were near null; marker E is the remaining arbitrary binary control before deciding whether any constructed marker encodes meaningful structure or merely serves as a negative control. Second, I request library-context main effects for the accepted associations: Avana-restricted SMARCA2/SMARCA4, WRN/MSI-high, and NFE2L2/KEAP1 effects (H73, H74, H75), plus KY-restricted SMARCA2/SMARCA4 and NFE2L2/KEAP1 effects (H76, H77). I omit a KY-restricted WRN analysis because MSI-high is a small exposed subgroup and the KY-exposed cell could be too imprecise; Avana is the dominant library, while KY provides a second platform check for the two larger binary exposures. Third, I request targeted moderation tests: growth-rate median-split interactions for SMARCA2/SMARCA4 and WRN/MSI-high (H80, H81), mutation-burden median-split interaction for WRN/MSI-high (H84), and STK11 co-loss interaction for NFE2L2/KEAP1 (H92). These test whether the accepted effects are stable across proliferation context, whether the WRN association is merely a proxy for hypermutation, and whether the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is robust to KEAP1-STK11 co-loss structure. I defer media-serum main effects, ploidy interactions, library-interaction tests, marker-E interactions, and remaining driver/MYC hypotheses until after these more direct robustness checks. Near-null marker-E or moderation tests, and consistent library-subset effects, would strengthen the conclusion that the accepted associations are meaningful dataset-level signals rather than artifacts of marker encoding, library platform, proliferation, mutation burden, or co-loss context. All selected contrasts remain associations within this dataset; no causal or external-validity claim is implied.

This wave provides strong robustness evidence for the three accepted large associations and completes the constructed-marker negative-control suite. Marker-E main effects are all close to zero for SMARCA2, WRN, and NFE2L2 (H34/H35/H36). Combined with the earlier marker-D and marker-F null controls, these results make it less plausible that the very large accepted signals are artifacts of the arbitrary constructed-marker encoding or marker-correlated structure; I therefore reject the marker-E association claims and close them. Library-restricted main effects are highly concordant with the overall effects. SMARCA4 loss predicts much stronger SMARCA2 dependency in both the dominant Avana library and the KY library, and MSI-high predicts much stronger WRN dependency in Avana. KEAP1 loss again predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency in both Avana and KY. These library-specific effects are large and precise, so I accept H73-H77 as context-specific dataset associations and close them. Moderation tests are less supportive of an important effect-size interaction. The growth-rate interaction for SMARCA4/SMARCA2 (H80) is statistically marginal but opposite to the registered negative direction; raw interaction is small and positive, not practically meaningful compared with the main effect near -0.8, so I reject H80 rather than promoting an opposite small interaction. The growth-rate interaction for MSI-high/WRN (H81) is imprecise and does not support the registered negative direction. The mutation-burden interaction for MSI-high/WRN (H84) is invalid because the low-burden complement contains no MSI-high cells; this indicates structural overlap between MSI status and mutation burden in this dataset rather than a meaningful null interaction. The STK11 co-loss interaction for KEAP1/NFE2L2 (H92) is near null and does not support direction-specific moderation. I request independent validation for H26, the TP53-loss-specific KEAP1/NFE2L2 association, because it is an accepted large context effect not yet independently validated and validating it would complete the KEAP1/NFE2L2 assessment across both TP53 strata.

The new validation evidence confirms both due claims and strengthens the core set of supported dataset-specific associations. For H7, SMARCA4 loss versus SMARCA4 intact in dependency_SMARCA2, the independent validation R26 is signed positive for the registered negative-direction claim: estimate +0.8006 with an independent interval [0.7713, 0.8300]. Because estimates are already signed to the hypothesis direction, the raw interpretation is that SMARCA4-loss lines have much more negative dependency_SMARCA2 scores than SMARCA4-intact lines, i.e. much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Discovery R7 and validation R26 are highly concordant in magnitude and direction, so H7 remains accepted and closed. For H26, KEAP1 loss versus KEAP1 intact in dependency_NFE2L2 within TP53-loss cells, validation R53 is signed positive for the registered positive-direction claim: estimate +0.8046 with an independent interval [0.7383, 0.8708]. The raw interpretation is that TP53-loss KEAP1-loss cells have less negative dependency_NFE2L2 scores than TP53-loss KEAP1-intact cells, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. This is consistent with discovery R25 and with the independently validated TP53-intact conditional claim H20, where R40 estimated a very similar effect. Thus the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is large in both TP53 strata and is independently validated for the TP53-loss stratum. Overall, the strongest evidence now supports three large associations in this supplied dataset: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, and KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The latter has been validated both overall as a reversed claim H19 and in TP53-intact H20 and TP53-loss H26 strata. Negative or null robustness evidence also constrains interpretation: constructed marker D/E/F main effects and interactions are near null; ARID1A loss is not associated with SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-intact cells; BRCA2 loss is not associated with WRN dependency among MSI-negative cells; and batch, lineage-subtype, culture, and library subset checks have not materially overturned the main effects. Remaining uncertainty concerns whether the large associations depend on culture media, Cas9 activity, ploidy, other co-mutations, or molecular context, and whether other measured predictors or subgroups show scientifically meaningful differences. The next most informative analyses are formal interaction tests for the accepted effects across additional technical and culture contexts, completion of the registered media-serum and Cas9 stress tests, TP53 interaction testing for KEAP1/NFE2L2, and broader driver/MYC hypothesis tests such as KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2, MYC, RB1, PIK3CA, and DNA-repair predictors. All conclusions should be interpreted as associations within this supplied dataset, not causal effects or externally generalizable findings.

No assessments are due, so I register new scientifically motivated comparisons while preserving existing unresolved robustness checks. The prior run established three very large dataset associations, but most other measured predictors remain either small or untested. I therefore add targeted biology and robustness questions.

First, I test MDM2 dependency through the p14ARF/MTAP/CDKN2A axis restricted to TP53-intact cells. CDKN2A encodes p14ARF, which inhibits MDM2; loss of CDKN2A could increase MDM2 pathway activity and therefore stronger MDM2 dependency, represented by a more negative dependency_MDM2 score. I register CDKN2A-loss versus CDKN2A-intact and MTAP-loss versus MTAP-intact in TP53-intact cells, both expected negative. MTAP is frequently co-deleted near CDKN2A and can proxy similar p14ARF/CDKN2A locus biology, so concordance would support a coherent axis; a large CDKN2A-only effect would favor CDKN2A-specific structure.

Second, I test more biologically selected RAS-pathway and RTK hypotheses. Direct KRAS-mutant versus wild-type effects were tiny, so I ask whether NF1 loss in KRAS-wild-type cells predicts stronger KRAS dependency. NF1 loss activates RAS signaling, and in the absence of KRAS mutation this may reveal dependency on endogenous KRAS signaling. I also test ERBB2 amplification among KRAS-wild-type cells because KRAS mutation can bypass EGFR/ERBB2 dependence; an association in KRAS-wild-type cells would be more informative for RTK dependency than an unselected analysis.

Third, I refine MYC hypotheses. Amplification alone may be too blunt, so I restrict MYC-amplification effects to cells above a high MYC-expression threshold. DHX9, USP7, POLR2A, and RPL11 are plausible MYC-associated vulnerabilities involving replication stress, protein stability, transcription, and translation. If MYC amplification is a biologically meaningful driver state only when accompanied by high MYC expression, these expression-restricted effects may be larger than the near-null amplification-only effects. If they remain small, MYC amplification is unlikely to be a strong predictor of these dependencies in this dataset.

Fourth, I add specificity and robustness checks for the accepted KEAP1/NFE2L2 signal. The prior STK11 co-loss interaction was near null, but a main effect restricted to STK11-intact cells can test whether the large positive effect is an artifact of KEAP1-STK11 co-deletion. I register KEAP1 loss versus KEAP1 intact among STK11-intact cells, with the registered positive direction matching the accepted weaker-NFE2L2-dependency association.

Finally, I test screen-quality moderation using screen_roc_auc median split. For accepted SMARCA2 and WRN effects, a near-null interaction would support stability; a more negative interaction would suggest stronger associations in higher-quality screens. For the KEAP1/NFE2L2 positive association, I use positive interaction direction for the same logic. These are dataset-level robustness checks, not external-validity claims.

I prioritize comparisons with adequate expected cell counts and avoid structurally impossible strata. Large, precise main effects would motivate later validation; near-zero MYC or screen-quality interactions would mainly narrow the space of additional predictors and support robustness of the accepted associations. All claims remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable findings.

No assessments are due, so I use the analysis slot to test the twelve newly registered high-specificity hypotheses rather than repeating already-tested comparisons. H99 and H100 test MDM2 dependency through p14ARF/CDKN2A and MTAP biology specifically in TP53-intact cells, where p53 pathway activity can make MDM2 dependency biologically interpretable. H101 tests whether NF1 loss in KRAS-wildtype cells predicts stronger KRAS dependency, a more biologically selected test than the weak overall KRAS-mutant contrast already observed. H102 tests ERBB2 amplification in KRAS-wildtype cells, where RTK dependence is less likely to be masked by KRAS-mutant bypass signaling. H103-H106 test MYC-amplification effects restricted to high MYC expression for DHX9, USP7, POLR2A, and RPL11, refining the near-null amplification-only MYC hypotheses. H107 tests the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association in STK11-intact cells to assess whether the large accepted effect is robust to KEAP1-STK11 co-deletion structure. Finally, H108-H110 test screen-quality moderation for the three accepted large associations using screen_roc_auc median split; near-null interactions would support robustness, while directionally large interactions would indicate dependence on screen quality. These analyses remain dataset-specific associations and not causal claims.

This wave mostly strengthens the robustness picture while producing one new biologically interesting MDM2 result and one unexpected opposite KRAS result. H99 is the strongest new finding: among TP53-intact cells, CDKN2A loss is associated with substantially stronger MDM2 dependency. The signed estimate is +0.1185 with CI [0.0793, 0.1577], meaning the raw CDKN2A-loss minus intact difference is approximately -0.119, i.e. more negative dependency. Relative to the MDM2 dependency mean magnitude (~0.269), even the lower bound is about a 29% difference, well above the 10% clinical-significance threshold. I accept H99 and request independent validation because it is a new, precise, mechanistically plausible association not yet externally checked in this run. H107 confirms that the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is not an artifact of STK11 co-loss: among STK11-intact cells, KEAP1 loss still shows a very large positive signed effect (+0.801, CI [0.779, 0.823]) for weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Given the already accepted and validated KEAP1/NFE2L2 main and TP53-stratified claims, I accept and close this as a context-specific robustness association. H100 remains unresolved because the MTAP-loss point effect is small (~+0.024 signed; raw stronger by 0.024, ~9% of MDM2 mean magnitude), but the upper CI bound allows a clinically meaningful effect. H101 rejects the registered prediction that NF1 loss in KRAS-wild-type cells predicts stronger KRAS dependency; the interval is entirely negative for the signed hypothesis direction, implying raw exposed-minus-comparator is positive/less negative, i.e. weaker KRAS dependency. That opposite effect is statistically clear and roughly 16% of the KRAS mean magnitude at the point estimate, so I reject the original claim and register a reversed post-hoc claim linked to H101 for future investigation. H102 is rejected because ERBB2 amplification in KRAS-wild-type cells shows a near-null interval whose positive tail is below the 10% threshold for dependency_ERBB2. The MYC high-expression restrictions mostly reject the stronger-dependency hypotheses: DHX9, POLR2A, and RPL11 effects are near zero and their positive tails are below 10% of the respective outcome means. USP7 is left unresolved/deferred because the interval is wide enough to include clinically meaningful effects in either direction, despite the point estimate being near zero. The screen-quality interactions H108-H110 do not support important moderation; their signed estimates are small and their intervals, evaluated relative to the very large main effects they moderate, do not indicate a meaningful interaction. They therefore support stability of the accepted SMARCA4/SMARCA2, MSI/WRN, and KEAP1/NFE2L2 associations. I also close the already accepted context claims H21 and H22 because they are sufficiently characterized as dataset-specific context associations. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset and not causal or externally generalizable effects.

This synthesis reassesses the two response-deadline validations and the new independent validation for the CDKN2A/MDM2 association. All three are concordant and strengthen the supported dataset-specific finding set. H9 is explicitly reassessed using discovery R8 and validation R39. For the registered negative-direction claim that MSI-high cells have stronger WRN dependency, the independent validation is signed positive: estimate +0.8215, interval [0.7661, 0.8768]. Because estimates are already signed, this means the raw MSI-high-minus-non-MSI-high contrast is strongly negative, i.e. much more negative dependency_WRN and therefore much stronger WRN dependency. The magnitude is enormous relative to the WRN dependency mean of about -0.301; even the validation lower bound is far above the 10% clinical-significance threshold. Discovery R8 (+0.7899) and validation R39 are highly concordant, so H9 remains accepted and closed. H20 is reassessed using discovery R24 and validation R40. Among TP53-intact cells, KEAP1 loss versus KEAP1 intact predicts weaker NFE2L2 dependency; validation is signed positive +0.7948, interval [0.7637, 0.8259], meaning the raw KEAP1-loss contrast is strongly positive and less negative, i.e. weaker dependency. This is essentially identical to discovery and far exceeds the 10% threshold. It also aligns with the independently validated TP53-loss stratum H26, making the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association large and robust across TP53 context. H99 is now accepted on independent validation. Among TP53-intact cells, CDKN2A loss versus intact predicts stronger MDM2 dependency; validation is signed positive +0.1162, interval [0.0584, 0.1741]. The raw interpretation is a negative MDM2 dependency difference of about 0.116, i.e. more negative dependency in CDKN2A-loss cells. The validation lower bound is about 22% of the MDM2 dependency mean magnitude, comfortably above the 10% clinical-significance threshold, and discovery R54 (+0.1185) is concordant. I therefore accept H99 and close its investigation as a validated dataset-specific association. Overall supported findings: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high status is associated with much stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency; and CDKN2A loss in TP53-intact cells is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency. The first three have independent validation and extensive context checks. The KEAP1/NFE2L2 association is robust across TP53-intact, TP53-loss, STK11-intact, library, and constructed-marker negative-control checks. The CDKN2A/MDM2 result is newly independently validated and mechanistically plausible through p14ARF/CDKN2A biology, although its dependence on MTAP co-deletion remains unresolved. Negative or null findings remain important: constructed marker D/E/F effects and many interactions are near null; ARID1A loss is not associated with SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-intact cells; BRCA2 loss is not associated with WRN dependency among MSI-negative cells; ERBB2 amplification in KRAS-wild-type cells does not show a clinically meaningful effect; high-expression-restricted MYC-amplification effects on DHX9, POLR2A, and RPL11 are not supported; screen-quality, batch, culture, growth-rate, and several co-mutation interactions do not materially overturn the large main effects. The direct driver-marker effects tested so far, including KRAS mutation overall, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2, and TP53 for MDM2, are generally small or not clinically meaningful in this dataset. Unresolved uncertainty remains for MTAP-independent effects, CDKN2A/MDM2 specificity in the absence of MTAP co-loss, whether CDKN2A effects persist when TP53 is lost, the post-hoc reversed NF1/KRAS observation, USP7 under high MYC expression, and many registered media, Cas9, ploidy, mutation-burden, and driver-context interactions. The most informative next analyses are the newly registered MDM2 specificity/TP53-context tests and the NF1/KRAS adenocarcinoma consistency test, followed by completing robustness interactions for the validated large effects and any already registered unresolved biological hypotheses. All conclusions remain associations within the supplied dataset, not causal effects or externally generalizable claims.

No assessments are due, so this stage registers a new wave of targeted biological and specificity tests around the validated core associations and around outcomes that remain weakly characterized. The accepted large associations are SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and CDKN2A loss among TP53-intact cells with stronger MDM2 dependency. The new proposals focus on the next most informative mechanisms and contexts. First, the CDKN2A/MDM2 result points to the p53-MDM2-USP7 axis. TP53 loss may weaken USP7 dependency because USP7 function is tied to the MDM2-p53 circuit, and CDKN2A loss among TP53-intact cells may also predict stronger USP7 dependency if p14ARF pathway effects extend across MDM2-regulating vulnerabilities. I also register TP53-loss, media-serum, and lineage-subtype context checks for the CDKN2A/MDM2 association. The TP53 interaction is particularly important because a near-null or positive interaction would support p14ARF specificity, whereas a large opposite-direction effect would indicate that the accepted TP53-intact association does not generalize across p53 context. The media and lineage checks are robustness/context tests, not external claims. Second, the unexpected post-hoc NF1/KRAS result showed weaker KRAS dependency with NF1 loss in KRAS-wild-type cells. I register a more restrictive KRAS-wild-type/BRAF-wild-type test to see whether that opposite association survives removal of other MAPK drivers. Because KRAS, BRAF, and RAS-pathway dependencies can be bypassed by alternative RAS activation, this may be more interpretable than the broader KRAS-wild-type analysis. Third, NF1 loss could also shift dependency within the RAS network; I register NF1 loss among KRAS-wild-type cells against RIT1 dependency, expecting stronger RIT1 dependency if endogenous RAS-pathway activation compensates for weaker KRAS dependency. Fourth, EGFR amplification effects were near threshold, so I test EGFR amplification among PIK3CA-wild-type cells. PIK3CA mutation may bypass EGFR dependence, making EGFR-amplified cells without PIK3CA mutation more likely to show clinically meaningful EGFR dependency. Fifth, direct driver-marker analyses for STAT3, DHX9, and USP7 remain sparse. PIK3CA mutation was near null for STAT3, so PTEN loss provides a complementary PI3K/AKT-pathway hypothesis, and SMAD4 loss provides a TGF-beta/noncanonical STAT3 hypothesis. BRCA2 loss is tested against DHX9 dependency because replication stress and helicase-related vulnerabilities are plausible but not yet supported in this dataset. These proposals are chosen to have binary exposures with adequate expected cell sizes and to test hypotheses where a 10-percent relative effect would be scientifically meaningful. All remain associations in the supplied dataset, not causal effects or generalizable claims.

No assessments are due, so I request twelve previously registered comparisons that are most informative now. First, the accepted CDKN2A/MDM2 association in TP53-intact cells needs specificity and context analysis. H112 tests whether the same CDKN2A-loss effect persists when TP53 is lost. If the effect disappears in TP53-loss cells, that supports a p14ARF/TP53-specific mechanism; if it persists, p53 may not be required or the association may reflect a broader genomic effect. H113 tests CDKN2A loss among TP53-intact and MTAP-intact cells to determine whether the CDKN2A association is specific rather than driven by nearby MTAP co-deletion. H114 tests MTAP loss among TP53-intact and CDKN2A-intact cells to assess whether MTAP has an independent effect on MDM2 dependency. H124 quantifies the TP53-context interaction directly, giving an estimate of whether CDKN2A affects MDM2 dependency differently in TP53-loss versus TP53-intact cells. Second, I extend the p53-MDM2 axis to USP7, another regulator of p53/MDM2 biology. H118 tests TP53-loss versus TP53-intact cells for weaker USP7 dependency, and H119 tests CDKN2A loss among TP53-intact cells for stronger USP7 dependency, allowing me to determine whether the MDM2 result is part of a broader p14ARF/p53-USP7 circuit or is MDM2-specific. Third, the unexpected NF1-loss versus KRAS-dependency observation needs independent-style consistency checks within this dataset. H115 tests the reversed NF1-loss effect among adenocarcinoma KRAS-wild-type cells, while H123 tests it among KRAS-wild-type cells that are also BRAF-wild-type, removing a major MAPK driver bypass. H121 tests NF1 loss among KRAS-wild-type cells for stronger RIT1 dependency, addressing whether reduced KRAS dependency is accompanied by compensatory dependency on another RAS-family node. Fourth, I test selected pathway-specific hypotheses that could reveal clinically meaningful effects masked in unselected analyses: EGFR amplification among PIK3CA-wild-type cells, where downstream bypass is less likely; BRCA2 loss for DHX9 dependency, a plausible replication-stress vulnerability; and PTEN loss for STAT3 dependency, a PI3K/AKT-STAT3 hypothesis after the PIK3CA result was near null. All selected analyses are existing claims and use the supplied dataset only. These are associations, not causal claims or external generalizability claims. If any effect is directionally coherent and its uncertainty is compatible with a clinically meaningful relative difference, I will consider it in appraise; if it is new, precise, and mechanistically important, I may then consider validation.

This wave produces two new very large dataset-specific associations and clarifies the CDKN2A/MDM2 result. H118 is the largest new finding: TP53 loss versus TP53 intact shows a strongly positive signed association with dependency_USP7 for the registered weaker-dependency direction, estimate +0.396 with 95% interval [0.325, 0.467]. Since estimates are already signed, the raw TP53-loss minus intact difference is positive, i.e. less negative dependency and therefore weaker USP7 dependency. Relative to the USP7 dependency mean magnitude (~0.175), the lower bound is roughly 1.9 times the mean, far above the 10% clinical-significance threshold. This is mechanistically plausible because USP7 is closely tied to p53/MDM2 biology, and p53 loss could reduce dependency on USP7. I accept H118 and request independent validation because it is a new, precise, mechanistically important claim. H116 is also a new large effect: PTEN loss versus PTEN intact shows a strong positive signed association for stronger STAT3 dependency, estimate +0.267, interval [0.215, 0.319]. Relative to the STAT3 dependency mean magnitude (~0.282), the lower bound is about 76% of the mean, so the evidence supports a clinically meaningful direction. I accept H116 and keep it active for context checks; PTEN/STAT3 is biologically plausible but less directly supported by prior negative STAT3 tests than the p53-USP7 finding. H112 shows that the CDKN2A-loss association with stronger MDM2 dependency also appears among TP53-loss cells: signed estimate +0.111, interval [0.035, 0.186], with lower bound about 13% of the MDM2 mean. I accept H112 as a robust context-specific dataset association and close that stratum. H113 shows the CDKN2A-loss MDM2 association among TP53-intact and MTAP-intact cells: signed estimate +0.106, interval [0.063, 0.149], lower bound about 23%. I accept H113 and close it as evidence that the accepted H99 result is not simply due to MTAP co-deletion. However, H124, the direct TP53-loss interaction, is near zero: signed estimate +0.008, interval [-0.077, 0.093]. The point estimate does not support a clinically meaningful interaction, but the interval is wide enough to allow important interaction in either direction, so I leave H124 unresolved and active. This means the CDKN2A/MDM2 association may not be p14ARF/TP53-specific in this dataset, contrary to a simple mechanistic expectation. H114 tests MTAP loss among TP53-intact and CDKN2A-intact cells; the signed effect is small, +0.009, interval [-0.015, 0.033]. The upper bound slightly exceeds a 10% threshold, but the point estimate is near null and the interval includes no effect, so I leave it unresolved rather than accepting or rejecting it. H119 tests whether the p14ARF/CDKN2A axis also predicts USP7 dependency among TP53-intact cells; the signed effect is essentially null, +0.003, interval [-0.019, 0.025]. The upper bound is near threshold and the point is negligible, so H119 is unresolved and deferred rather than accepted. The RIT1 test is negative for the proposed compensatory mechanism: H121 rejects the hypothesis that NF1 loss among KRAS-wild-type cells strengthens RIT1 dependency; the signed estimate is -0.011 and the upper bound for the proposed direction is below the 10% threshold. The NF1/KRAS post-hoc observation remains suggestive but not acceptably precise: H123 is positive, +0.036, interval [0.003, 0.069], but the lower bound is far below the 10% threshold; H115 in adenocarcinoma includes null. Thus I keep H115 and H123 active/unresolved rather than accepting. EGFR amplification among PIK3CA-wild-type cells (H122) is in the expected direction but has a lower CI bound near null; BRCA2 loss for DHX9 (H120) is near null with an upper bound that still allows a meaningful effect. Both remain unresolved. Overall, the new accepted evidence strengthens a p53-related USP7 association and adds PTEN loss as a strong STAT3 dependency association, while showing CDKN2A/MDM2 is robust to MTAP-intact restriction and also present in the TP53-loss stratum. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal claims or generalizable claims.

H26 is reassessed using the independent validation response. The claim is that, among TP53-loss cells, KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Discovery R25 and validation R53 are highly concordant: signed estimates are about +0.810 and +0.805, with validation interval [0.738, 0.871]. Because the claim direction is +1, these positive signed values mean the raw KEAP1-loss contrast is strongly positive, i.e. less negative dependency and therefore much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Even the validation lower bound is vastly above the 10% clinical-significance threshold. H26 remains accepted and closed as a robust dataset-specific KEAP1/NFE2L2 association within the TP53-loss stratum. H118 is now independently validated. The claim is that TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency. Discovery R71 (+0.396, interval [0.325, 0.467]) and validation R79 (+0.380, interval [0.269, 0.491]) are concordant and signed in the hypothesized direction. The raw TP53-loss contrast is positive, i.e. less negative USP7 dependency, and the validation lower bound is far above 10% of the USP7 dependency mean magnitude. This is mechanistically coherent because USP7 function is tied to the p53/MDM2 circuit, and p53 loss could reduce dependency on USP7. I therefore accept H118 and close the main claim, while separately registered context and interaction tests can characterize robustness and specificity. H109 tested whether the large MSI-high/WRN association is moderated by screen quality, using high screen ROC as the subgroup. The signed point estimates are tiny and in the opposite direction of the registered interaction: discovery R64 is about -0.0004 and validation R80 is about -0.0118. Both intervals include null, and the validation interval is wide because the subsplit reduces MSI-high cells. I interpret the combined evidence as no positive support for the pre-specified screen-quality moderation. The interval still allows residual uncertainty, but this is a low-priority technical robustness check rather than a biologically important discovered interaction, so I keep H109 rejected and closed. Overall supported dataset-specific findings now include: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, robust across TP53-intact and TP53-loss strata; CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency, validated in TP53-intact cells and also supported in TP53-loss and MTAP-intact strata; newly validated TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency; and PTEN loss with much stronger STAT3 dependency, accepted but still awaiting context checks. Negative or unsupported findings include no support for NF1-loss strengthening RIT1 dependency in KRAS-wild-type cells, no support for strong CDKN2A-loss/USP7 effects among TP53-intact cells, and no support for meaningful screen-quality moderation of the MSI/WRN association. The most informative next analyses are USP7 context and interaction tests around TP53 loss, STAT3 context tests around PTEN loss, completion of the MDM2 CDKN2A/TP53/MTAP specificity grid, and broadening to DHX9 TP53-loss dependency. All conclusions remain associations in the supplied dataset, not causal effects or externally generalizable claims.

No assessments are due. This corrected explore form registers refinements and new comparisons without leaving refinements in an invalid state: whenever a proposal is linked to an earlier parent, I attach available motivating result IDs. For proposals whose parent had no direct evidence, such as the KIF18A/RB1 follow-up, I intentionally omit the parent link and register the context test as a new comparison. The scientific plan has two purposes. First, it checks whether the strongest accepted dataset-specific associations remain robust in biologically meaningful contexts: PTEN loss and STAT3 in adenocarcinoma and high IFN-gamma; TP53 loss and USP7 in high MYC-expression cells; CDKN2A loss and MDM2 in PTEN-intact cells; MSI-high and WRN in high IFN-gamma; SMARCA4 loss and SMARCA2 in high AXL; KEAP1 loss and NFE2L2 in high hypoxia. These are not causal or external-validity claims, but they ask whether the large effects are general within the supplied dataset or are tied to specific biological states. Second, it broadens exploration to underexplored driver and pathway hypotheses where a 10% relative difference would be scientifically useful: EGFR amplification among STK11-intact cells, ERBB2 amplification among EGFR-intact cells, KRAS mutation among TP53-intact cells, RB1 loss among rapidly growing cells for KIF18A, and BRCA2 loss for POLR2A. All proposed exposure contrasts use variables with adequate expected cell sizes and clear exposed/comparator definitions. The analysis stage should select the most informative subset of these registered claims.

No assessments are due. I request twelve existing registered comparisons that best balance focused follow-up and broad discovery. First, PTEN loss has emerged as a strong new association with stronger STAT3 dependency. I test its specificity and robustness across three mechanistically meaningful contexts: TP53-intact cells (H128), PIK3CA-wild-type cells where downstream bypass is less likely (H132), and adenocarcinoma subtype (H136). Second, TP53 loss has been validated as a strong association with weaker USP7 dependency. I characterize robustness and potential specificity using the dominant Avana library (H127), MTAP-intact cells (H130), and a direct interaction with CDKN2A loss (H131), which can determine whether the USP7 effect is partly overlapping with the p14ARF/CDKN2A/MDM2 axis. Third, I complete MDM2 specificity checks around the accepted CDKN2A-loss association by asking whether the effect is invariant across lineage subtype (H126) and whether it persists among PTEN-intact cells (H139). Fourth, I broaden beyond accepted markers to underexplored DNA-repair, transcription, and mitosis hypotheses: SMAD4 loss versus STAT3 dependency (H117), TP53 loss versus DHX9 dependency (H135), RB1 loss among faster-growing cells versus KIF18A dependency (H146), and BRCA2 loss versus POLR2A dependency (H147). These tests are still associations within the supplied dataset only and do not imply causality or external generalizability.

This appraise wave mostly tests robustness and specificity of previously accepted associations, and the central accepted associations remain strong. For PTEN loss and stronger STAT3 dependency, the effect is robust in three contexts: TP53-intact cells (H128, signed +0.287 [0.227,0.347]), PIK3CA-wild-type cells (H132, signed +0.267 [0.210,0.323]), and adenocarcinoma cells (H136, signed +0.268 [0.206,0.330]). The lower bounds are all many times the 10% absolute-mean benchmark for dependency_STAT3 (~0.282), so these are strong dataset-specific associations rather than fragile context artifacts. For TP53 loss and weaker USP7 dependency, the effect is robust in the dominant Avana library (H127, signed +0.405 [0.330,0.479]) and in MTAP-intact cells (H130, signed +0.421 [0.343,0.498]), far above the 10% benchmark for dependency_USP7 (~0.175). For CDKN2A loss and stronger MDM2 dependency, the association remains strong in PTEN-intact cells (H139, signed +0.116 [0.078,0.153]), again above the 10% benchmark for dependency_MDM2 (~0.269). These context acceptances should be interpreted as robustness checks within the supplied dataset, not as mechanistic causality claims.

The direct interaction tests are less decisive. The USP7 TP53-loss effect does not show evidence of moderation by CDKN2A loss (H131, signed -0.004 [-0.177,0.170]); the interval is wide and allows clinically meaningful interaction in either direction, so this remains unresolved rather than rejected. The CDKN2A/MDM2 lineage interaction is also near null and imprecise (H126, signed -0.010 [-0.088,0.068]); the accepted CDKN2A/MDM2 association does not require lineage-specific moderation, so I defer further follow-up. SMAD4 loss and STAT3 dependency is near null with wide uncertainty (H117, signed +0.011 [-0.026,0.047]); the upper bound allows a meaningful effect, but the evidence is not supportive, so it is deferred.

H135 is rejected as originally registered: TP53 loss was not associated with stronger DHX9 dependency. The signed interval is entirely negative, meaning the raw contrast is positive (TP53 loss associated with weaker DHX9 dependency), but the raw magnitude interval is small (~0.001 to 0.039) and only the upper portion crosses the 10% benchmark for dependency_DHX9. I therefore do not accept the opposite direction, but I register it as a new exploratory reversal linked to H135 because the raw interval is on one side of zero. H146 and H147 are inconclusive: RB1 loss among faster-growing cells and BRCA2 loss for POLR2A have intervals that include both null and potentially meaningful effects, but point estimates are small; I defer them. Overall, the most important pending action is independent validation of the main PTEN/STAT3 association (H116), which remains unvalidated despite strong context support.

Final synthesis at this checkpoint focuses on the two due validation results and then places them within the broader evidence set.

H99 is accepted and closed. The hypothesis is that CDKN2A loss is associated with more negative MDM2 dependency score, i.e. stronger MDM2 dependency, among TP53-intact cells. Because the claim direction is -1, the positive signed estimates mean the raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast is negative. Discovery R54 estimated +0.1185 [0.0793, 0.1577]; independent validation R66 estimated +0.1162 [0.0584, 0.1741]. These are highly concordant in magnitude and precision. Relative to the average absolute MDM2 dependency score, the validation lower bound is far above the 10% practical benchmark, and the point estimate is very large in dependency-score units. This is one of the most robust dataset-specific associations discovered: CDKN2A-loss cells show stronger MDM2 dependency, with consistency across TP53-intact, TP53-loss, MTAP-intact, and PTEN-intact contexts.

H116 is accepted and closed. The hypothesis is that PTEN loss is associated with more negative STAT3 dependency score, i.e. stronger STAT3 dependency. With direction -1, the positive signed estimates indicate the raw contrast is in the hypothesized direction. Discovery R78 estimated +0.2674 [0.2153, 0.3195]; independent validation R93 estimated +0.2770 [0.1967, 0.3572]. The validation lower bound remains far above 10% of the average absolute STAT3 dependency score, and the effect is stable in TP53-intact, PIK3CA-wild-type, and adenocarcinoma contexts. I therefore treat PTEN loss as a strongly supported predictor of stronger STAT3 dependency within this supplied dataset, without implying causality or external generalizability.

Supported dataset-specific findings now center on five biologically coherent axes: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, robust across TP53-intact and TP53-loss strata and several context subsets; CDKN2A loss with stronger MDM2 dependency, independently validated and robust across p53/MTAP/PTEN contexts; TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, independently validated and robust in the dominant library and MTAP-intact strata; and PTEN loss with much stronger STAT3 dependency, now independently validated and robust across TP53-intact, PIK3CA-wild-type, and adenocarcinoma contexts.

Negative or unsupported findings include: no support for the original hypothesis that NF1 loss strengthens KRAS dependency among KRAS-wild-type cells, and no support that NF1 loss strengthens RIT1 dependency in the same setting; no support that MYC amplification is a simple predictor of stronger POLR2A, RPL11, DHX9, or USP7 dependency; no meaningful association of the arbitrary research markers D/E/F with SMARCA2, WRN, or NFE2L2 dependency; and little evidence that technical screen-quality or batch-like variables strongly moderate the largest accepted biological associations, although some interaction intervals remain wide.

Unresolved uncertainty remains. The opposite-direction NF1-loss effects on KRAS dependency among KRAS-wild-type cells (H111/H123) have positive intervals but lower bounds below the practical 10% benchmark and are post-hoc relative to the original hypotheses, so they are deferred rather than accepted. The opposite-direction TP53-loss association with DHX9 dependency (H148) is similarly small and clinically uncertain. EGFR amplification in PIK3CA-wild-type cells (H122) shows an opposite-direction near-threshold signal, and the CDKN2A-loss/TP53-loss interaction for MDM2 (H124) and USP7 TP53-loss/CDKN2A-loss interaction (H131) are too imprecise to conclude effect modification. All conclusions remain associations in the supplied dataset only.

The most informative next analyses should refine and localize the accepted findings rather than repeatedly retest their overall existence. Overall final synthesis: The strongest and most reproducible findings are six broad association axes. (1) SMARCA4 loss is associated with very strong SMARCA2 dependency, replicated by independent validation and stable across many lineage, culture, library, molecular, and screen-QC contexts. (2) MSI-high status is associated with very strong WRN dependency, replicated and stable across overall, adenocarcinoma, adherent culture, Avana-library, aneuploidy, and hypoxia contexts. (3) KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, replicated and stable across TP53, STK11, MTAP, library, hypoxia, mutation-burden, and other contexts. (4) CDKN2A loss is associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, replicated and broadly stable across TP53 state, MTAP-loss contexts, aneuploidy, and several culture/library settings, though the genomic co-location of CDKN2A and MTAP limits biological specificity. (5) TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency, replicated and present across many molecular and technical strata. (6) PTEN loss is associated with stronger STAT3 dependency, replicated and stable across TP53 state, adenocarcinoma, PIK3CA, EMT, hypoxia, and mutation-burden strata.

Negative or unsupported findings are also substantial. Matched driver-gene dependency relationships were largely not supported: KRAS mutation did not establish stronger KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E was not meaningfully associated with BRAF dependency; EGFR amplification did not robustly support stronger EGFR dependency; and ERBB2 amplification did not support stronger ERBB2 dependency in the overall or key refined contexts. MYC amplification or high MYC-expression contexts did not support DHX9, POLR2A, RPL11, TMED10, or USP7 dependency. RB1 loss was not supported as a strong KIF18A dependency predictor, and CDKN2A loss was not associated with stronger KRAS or KIF18A dependency overall. The constructed research markers D, E, and F behaved as null panels. BRCA2 loss was not meaningful for WRN dependency among MSI-negative lines and is now also rejected for TP53-intact POLR2A dependency.

Remaining uncertainty is mainly about context modification rather than the main axes. Several formal interactions were zero-crossing or imprecise, including MTAP-loss modification of TP53-loss USP7 dependency, TP53-loss-by-CDKN2A-loss interaction for USP7, and PTEN-loss interaction/localization hypotheses for STAT3. Some CDKN2A/MDM2 co-loss contexts remain borderline or unresolved, especially STK11-loss and KEAP1-loss strata. These unresolved items are not enough to overturn the main accepted axes, but they prevent strong claims about biological specificity or causality.

Most informative next analyses should remain tightly targeted because no independent validation budget remains. The highest-value follow-ups are: complete the CDKN2A/MDM2 2x2 TP53-by-MTMP localization, especially TP53-loss MTAP-loss co-alteration lines; test formal TP53-by-MTAP and TP53-by-culture interactions for USP7 dependency; examine KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 lineage robustness with formal interaction tests where powered; and refine PTEN-loss STAT3 dependency in remaining molecular contexts only if sample sizes support it. Broad near-null rescanning of already-supported axes or already-unsupported matched-driver hypotheses would be less informative than these targeted mechanistic-context follow-ups.
